i OurBigBook.com
The linear Diophantine equation solvability criterion says that ax+by=c has an integer solution exactly when gcd(a,b) divides c. The Euclidean algorithm gives
231410073001078621​=2(1007)+300,=3(300)+107,=2(107)+86,=86+21,=4(21)+2,=10(2)+1.​
(1)
Thus gcd(1007,2314)=1, which divides 37. Therefore
1007x+2314y=37 has integer solutions.​
(2)

Applying the Euclidean algorithm,
3211250870339930495​=2508+703,=3(703)+399,=399+304,=304+95,=3(95)+19,=5(19).​
(3)
Hence gcd(2508,3211)=19. Since 19 does not divide 55, the linear Diophantine equation solvability criterion gives
2508x+3211y=55 has no integer solution.​

Words: 97 Articles: 1
1G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 97
iii OurBigBook.com
The quadratic form factors as a sum of two squares:
5x2+16xy+13y2=(x+2y)2+(2x+3y)2.
(5)
The change of variables
u=x+2y,v=2x+3y
(6)
has determinant −1, so its matrix is a unimodular matrix and it maps Z2 bijectively to itself. The original equation is therefore equivalent to
u2+v2=365.
(7)
The sum of two squares theorem also decides this systematically: 365=5⋅73, and every prime factor congruent to 3 modulo 4 occurs to an even power, vacuously here. Thus 365 is a sum of two integer squares. Explicitly,
365=22+192.
(8)
Inverting the change of variables gives, for example, (x,y)=(32,−15). Consequently
5x2+16xy+13y2=365 has integer solutions.​
(9)
This is the unimodular reduction of a discriminant-minus-four form to two squares.

The Liouville approximation theorem states that if α is an irrational algebraic number of degree d≥2, then there is a constant c(α)>0 such that every reduced rational p/q satisfies
​α−qp​​>qdc(α)​​.
(10)
Let P∈Z[X] be the minimal polynomial of α, of degree d. Since P is irreducible of degree greater than one, P(p/q)=0. Moreover,
qdP(p/q)∈Z∖{0},
(11)
and hence
∣P(p/q)∣≥q−d.
(12)
On the compact interval I=[α−1,α+1], put
M=maxx∈I​∣P′(x)∣.
(13)
If p/q∈I, the mean value theorem gives a point ξ between α and p/q such that
∣P(p/q)∣=∣P′(ξ)∣​qp​−α​≤M​qp​−α​.
(14)
Thus ∣α−p/q∣≥M−1q−d. If p/q∈/I, then ∣α−p/q∣>1≥q−d. Taking any
0<c(α)<min{1,M−1}
(15)
proves the stated strict inequality.

Since the positive series converges, an​→0. We construct the subsequence recursively. Choose n(1) arbitrarily. Once n(1)<⋯<n(k−1) have been chosen, write the reduced partial sums as
sj​=∑r=1j​an(r)​=qj​pj​​(1≤j<k).
(18)
Choose n(k)>n(k−1) so far out that
0<an(k)​<2−kmin1≤j<k​qj−j​.
(19)
This is possible because an​→0.
Let
α=∑k=1∞​an(k)​.
(20)
For every fixed j, each later choice includes qj−j​ in its minimum, so
0<α−sj​<qj−j​∑k=j+1∞​2−k=2−jqj−j​.
(21)
First, α is irrational. If α=u/v were reduced and rational, the strictly increasing rational sequence sj​→α would have unbounded denominators qj​; only finitely many reduced fractions in a bounded interval have bounded denominator. Choose j>2 with qj​>v. Part (b) would give
∣α−sj​∣>qj−2​,
(22)
contrary to ∣α−sj​∣<2−jqj−j​<qj−2​.
If α were algebraic of degree d, part (a) would give a constant c>0 with
∣α−sj​∣>cqj−d​.
(23)
For j>d our construction instead gives
∣α−sj​∣<2−jqj−j​≤2−jqj−d​,
(24)
which contradicts the lower bound once 2−j<c. Hence α is transcendental. This proves the transcendental subseries of a positive rational convergent series construction.

3I (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 297 Articles: 4
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 185 Articles: 1
3I OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 185
a OurBigBook.com
A binary code c:A→{0,1}∗ is a prefix code when no codeword is a proper prefix of another. If the source letters have probabilities p1​,…,pm​ and codeword lengths l1​,…,lm​, the expected value of its codeword length is
L=∑r=1m​pr​lr​.
(25)
It is an optimal prefix code when it minimizes L among all binary prefix codes for that source.
Suppose pi​>pj​ but li​>lj​. Exchanging the codewords assigned to μi​ and μj​ leaves the set of words, and hence prefix-freeness, unchanged. The change in expected length is
pi​lj​+pj​li​−(pi​li​+pj​lj​)=(pi​−pj​)(lj​−li​)<0,
(26)
contradicting optimality. Thus
pi​>pj​ ⟹ li​≤lj​​,
(27)
which is the probability monotonicity of optimal prefix-code lengths.
Represent the code by its binary prefix tree and choose a codeword wb of maximal length, where b∈{0,1}. Its sibling is w(1−b). If that sibling were not a codeword, it could not have a codeword below it either, since such a word would be longer than wb. Replacing wb by w would then preserve prefix-freeness and strictly reduce L. This is impossible for an optimal code, so w(1−b) is also a maximal-length codeword. The pair differs only in its last digit, proving the deepest sibling property of an optimal prefix code.

b OurBigBook.com
The Huffman coding merges may be chosen as
0.1+0.1=0.2,0.2+0.2=0.4,0.2+0.4=0.6,0.4+0.6=1.
(28)
Resolving the tied weights so that the original 0.4 symbol is merged only at the final step gives the code
probabilitycodeword​0.40​0.2100​0.2101​0.1110​0.1111.​​
(29)
Its lengths are (1,3,3,3,3) and its expected length is
0.4+3(0.2+0.2+0.1+0.1)=2.2​.
(30)
The Huffman coding theorem proves optimality, so an optimal coding with all but one word of the same length does exist. This is an instance of a nonunique optimal prefix code: a different resolution of the ties also gives the optimal profile (2,2,2,3,3).
An optimal code cannot have five distinct lengths. By the deepest sibling property of an optimal prefix code, at least two maximal-length codewords have the same length. Thus the answers are respectively
(i) yes,(ii) no​.
(31)

A→BC,A→a,

Take
G′=({a,b},{S,A,B},P′,S),
(37)
where
P′={S→ABA, A→AB, B→BA, A→a, B→b}.
(38)
This grammar is in Weak Chomsky normal form. In the original grammar, C occurs only in S→AC and has the sole production C→BA. Thus every use of
S→AC→ABA
(39)
is replaced in G′ by S→ABA, while every later production is unchanged. Conversely, the ternary production can always be expanded into those two original steps. Therefore G′ is equivalent to G in the sense of an equivalent grammar.

For X=x, the last flip must be the rth head. Among the preceding x+r−1 flips, exactly x are tails and r−1 are heads. There are (xx+r−1​) choices for their positions, and every resulting sequence has probability (1−p)xpr. The negative binomial stopping argument therefore gives
P(X=x)=(xx+r−1​)(1−p)xpr​,x=0,1,…,
(41)
so X has the failures-before-the-rth-success negative binomial distribution.
To put the mass function into exponential family form, set
θ=log(1−p),−∞<θ<0.
(42)
Since p=1−eθ,
Pθ​(X=x)=(xx+r−1​)exp{θx+rlog(1−eθ)}=h(x)exp{θT(x)−A(θ)},
(43)
where
T(x)=x​,A(θ)=−rlog(1−eθ)​,h(x)=(xx+r−1​).
(44)
Thus the natural parameter of an exponential family is θ, and the Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem shows that T(X)=X is a sufficient statistic. This is the negative binomial exponential family.
The exponential-family derivative identities now give
E[X]=A′(θ)=1−eθreθ​=pr(1−p)​​
(45)
and
var(X)=A′′(θ)=(1−eθ)2reθ​=p2r(1−p)​​.
(46)

With population n, the transition diagram has the two outgoing arrows
nλ​n+3,nβn​n−1.
(47)
Thus this is a batch-birth linear-death process. If Pn​(t)=P(Nt​=n) and Pj​=0 for j<0, probability enters state n from n−3 by a birth and from n+1 by a death. Hence the master equation is
P˙n​=λPn−3​+β(n+1)Pn+1​−(λ+βn)Pn​​.
(48)
The Markov jump-process generator is
(Lf)(n)=λ(f(n+3)−f(n))+βn(f(n−1)−f(n)).
(49)
For f(n)=n, this gives Ln=3λ−βn. Therefore the expected value m(t)=E[Nt​] satisfies
m′=3λ−βm,m(0)=n0​,
(50)
so
m(t)=β3λ​(1−e−βt)+n0​e−βt​.
(51)
For f(n)=n2,
Ln2=λ(6n+9)+βn(−2n+1).
(52)
Writing s=E[Nt2​] and using the generator identity gives
s′=6λm+9λ−2βs+βm.
(53)
The variance v=s−m2 consequently obeys
v′​=s′−2mm′=9λ+βm−2βv.​
(54)
If v(0)=v0​<∞, substitution of the formula for m yields
v(t)=v0​e−2βt+β6λ​(1−e−2βt)+(n0​−β3λ​)(e−βt−e−2βt).
(55)
All transient terms vanish, and the moments of a batch-birth linear-death process therefore give
var(Nt​)⟶β6λ​​.
(56)

Taking reciprocals in the finite product defining the gamma function gives
Γ(z)1​=zlimn→∞​n−z∏k=1n​(1+kz​).
(57)
Let Hn​=∑k=1n​k−1. Since
n−z=ez(Hn​−logn)e−zHn​=ez(Hn​−logn)∏k=1n​e−z/k
(58)
and Hn​−logn→γ, where γ is the Euler--Mascheroni constant, passage to the limit gives the Weierstrass product for the reciprocal gamma function
Γ(z)1​=zeγzk=1∏∞​(1+kz​)e−z/k​.
(59)
The logarithmic derivative of this identity is
−ψ(z)=z1​+γ+∑k=1∞​(z+k1​−k1​).
(60)
Since k−1−(z+k)−1=z/[k(z+k)], the digamma function therefore satisfies
ψ(z)=−γ−z1​+zk=1∑∞​k(z+k)1​​.
(61)
For real z>0, termwise differentiation gives the trigamma function
ψ′(z)=z21​+∑k=1∞​(z+k)21​>0.
(62)
Thus ψ is strictly increasing on the positive real axis. At the two positive integers needed here, telescoping gives
ψ(1)=−γ<0,ψ(2)=1−γ>0.
(63)
The intermediate value theorem supplies a zero in (1,2), and strict increase makes it unique. This is the positive zero of the digamma function.

L′−L=qdf/dt​.
(65)
The action changes only by q[f(t2​)−f(t1​)], whose variation vanishes for fixed endpoints. By total-time-derivative invariance of a Lagrangian, the Euler-Lagrange equation is unchanged.

A binary symmetric channel independently flips each input bit with probability p, so, with rows indexed by the input and columns by the output, its channel matrix is
(1−pp​p1−p​)​.

If p>1/2, complementing every received bit converts the channel into one with crossover probability 1−p<1/2 without changing its information-carrying ability. The case p=1/2 has identical rows and capacity zero, so it suffices to study p<1/2.
The Shannon second coding theorem states that for every rate below the channel capacity there are arbitrarily long codes whose decoding error tends to zero, whereas no sequence of codes with rate above capacity can have vanishing error. It also identifies
C=maxPX​​I(X;Y).

I(X;Y)=H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=H(Y)−h2​(p).
(98)

C=1−h2​(p)​

The compactness theorem says that a set T of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset of T has a model. One direction is immediate: a model of T models every subset. Conversely, suppose every finite subset is satisfiable. If T had no model, then T⊨⊥. The Godel completeness theorem would give a formal proof T⊢⊥. Every proof is finite, so it would use only a finite subset T0​⊆T, making T0​ inconsistent and hence unsatisfiable. This contradiction proves compactness.
The Upward Lowenheim-Skolem theorem says that a first-order theory with an infinite model has models of arbitrarily large cardinality. Fix a cardinal κ and expand the language by constants cα​ for α<κ. Add the sentences
cα​=cβ​(α=β)
(174)
to T. Any finite subset mentions only finitely many new constants, which can be interpreted as distinct elements of the given infinite model. Compactness therefore gives a model of the expanded theory in which the cα​ are all distinct. Its reduct is a model of T of cardinality at least κ. Together with the downward theorem, this gives a model of exactly κ whenever κ≥∣L∣+ℵ0​.
The Downward Lowenheim-Skolem theorem says that if A is an infinite L-structure and
∣L∣+ℵ0​≤κ≤∣A∣,
(175)
then A has an elementary substructure of cardinality κ. To see why, first choose κ elements. For every existential formula, add a Skolem function selecting a witness whenever one exists, and repeatedly close the chosen set under all language operations and these witness functions. There are at most κ functions of finite arity, so the closure still has size κ. Every existential statement true in A with parameters from the closure has a witness in the closure; the Tarski--Vaught test therefore says that the resulting substructure is elementary.

A finite extension L/K is normal when every irreducible polynomial in K[T] having one root in L splits completely over L.
Suppose first that L/K is normal. Choose α1​,…,αm​ with L=K(α1​,…,αm​), and let fj​ be the minimal polynomial of αj​ over K. Every fj​ splits in L by normality, and L is generated by their roots because it is already generated by the particular roots αj​. Thus L is the splitting field of f1​⋯fm​.
Conversely, suppose that L is the splitting field of f∈K[T]. Every K-embedding σ:L→K permutes the roots of f, so σ(L)=L. By the embedding characterization of normality, L/K is normal. This proves the finite normal extension as a splitting field criterion.

A complex representation of a finite group G is a homomorphism
ρ:G⟶GL(V)
(190)
for a finite-dimensional complex vector space V. It is an irreducible representation when its only invariant subspaces are 0 and V, and its degree is dimV. Two representations are isomorphic when there is an invertible linear map intertwining their G-actions.
Write the dihedral group as
D2n​=⟨r,s:rn=s2=1, srs=r−1⟩.
(191)
In an irreducible representation choose an eigenvector 0=v∈V of ρ(r), which is possible because rn=1. If its eigenvalue is λ, then
ρ(r)ρ(s)v=ρ(s)ρ(r)−1v=λ−1ρ(s)v.
(192)
Thus W=span{v,ρ(s)v} is invariant under both r and s. Irreducibility forces W=V, proving dimV≤2 as in irreducible complex representations of a finite dihedral group.
Let ω=e2πi/n. Besides the one-dimensional representations described below, define for each indicated j
ρj​(r)=(ωj0​0ω−j​),ρj​(s)=(01​10​).
(193)
These matrices satisfy the defining relations. Since ωj=ω−j, the only one-dimensional r-invariant subspaces are the two coordinate axes, and s interchanges them. Hence ρj​ is irreducible. Their characters satisfy
χj​(r)=2cosn2πj​,
(194)
whose values are distinct in the ranges below, so the ρj​ are pairwise nonisomorphic. This is the family of two-dimensional representations of a finite dihedral group.
If n is odd, a one-dimensional character must send r to a scalar ε satisfying εn=1 and ε=ε−1. Thus ε=1, while s may independently map to 1 or −1. These give two one-dimensional irreducibles. Taking
j=1,…,2n−1​
(195)
gives (n−1)/2 two-dimensional irreducibles, for a total of
2+2n−1​=2n+3​.
(196)
If n is even, r may map to either 1 or −1, and again s may map independently to either sign. This gives four pairwise nonisomorphic one-dimensional irreducibles. Taking
j=1,…,2n​−1
(197)
gives n/2−1 two-dimensional irreducibles, for a total of
4+(2n​−1)=2n+6​.
(198)
Different dimensions distinguish the one- and two-dimensional families, completing the required construction and justification.

The open mapping theorem states that every surjective bounded linear map S:X→Y between Banach spaces maps open sets to open sets. Equivalently, there is c>0 such that
BY​(0,c)⊆S(BX​(0,1)).
(216)
The closed graph theorem states that a linear map T:X→Y between Banach spaces is continuous if and only if its graph
Γ(T)={(x,Tx):x∈X}
(217)
is closed in X×Y.
Assume the open mapping theorem and suppose Γ(T) is closed. As a closed subspace of the Banach space X×Y, the graph is itself Banach. The coordinate projection
P:Γ(T)⟶X,(x,Tx)⟼x
(218)
is a bounded linear bijection. By the open mapping theorem, P−1 is bounded. The other coordinate projection Q:Γ(T)→Y is bounded, and
T=Q∘P−1.
(219)
Thus T is bounded and hence continuous. This is the closed graph theorem from the bounded inverse theorem argument.

so (fn​(v)) is Cauchy in the scalar field. Define f(v)=limn​fn​(v). Passing to limits in the linearity identities shows that f is linear.

A germ of a holomorphic function at z∈D is an equivalence class [f]z​ of pairs consisting of a neighbourhood U of z and a holomorphic function f:U→C. Two pairs represent the same germ if their functions agree on some neighbourhood of z.
The space of germs of holomorphic functions is
G={[f]z​:z∈D}.
(242)
For every holomorphic f on an open U⊆D, the set
Uf​={[f]z​:z∈U}
(243)
is declared open; these sets form a basis. The forgetful map
π:G→D,π([f]z​)=z,
(244)
maps each Uf​ homeomorphically onto U. The inverses of these restrictions give the charts defining the complex structure, so π is a local biholomorphism.
The evaluation map is
E:G→C,E([f]z​)=f(z).

An explicit gluing description is obtained by pairing the eight roots into four adjacent pairs and cutting the plane along four disjoint arcs joining the members of each pair. To compactify, first add one point above each of the eight roots of unity. These are simple branch points of the double cover. Since the polynomial has even degree eight, the even-degree hyperelliptic model has two distinct, unbranched points above infinity. Consequently

ℓ(t)=p+t(q−p)

For the density statement, embed an irreducible affine variety X of dimension d in An and choose generators f1​,…,fr​ of its ideal. By dimension from minimum tangent dimension, some point has tangent dimension d, so the Jacobian has rank n−d there. Some (n−d)×(n−d) minor Δ is consequently nonzero on X. The distinguished open set

Dynkin lemma, also called the pi-lambda theorem, states that if a Dynkin system D contains a pi-system P, then
σ(P)⊆D.
(275)
Let λ(P) be the smallest Dynkin system containing P. It is enough to prove that λ(P) is a sigma-algebra, because then
σ(P)⊆λ(P)⊆D.
(276)
First fix A∈P and define
GA​={B∈λ(P):A∩B∈λ(P)}.
(277)
This is a Dynkin system. It contains Ω because A∈λ(P); closure under relative complements follows from
A∩Bc=A∖(A∩B),
(278)
and closure under disjoint unions follows by distributing A∩− over the union. Since P is closed under intersections, P⊆GA​. Minimality therefore gives
λ(P)⊆GA​.
(279)
Thus A∩B∈λ(P) whenever A∈P and B∈λ(P).
Now fix B∈λ(P) and define
HB​={A∈λ(P):A∩B∈λ(P)}.
(280)
The same argument shows that HB​ is a Dynkin system, and the preceding paragraph shows that it contains P. Hence HB​=λ(P). We have proved that λ(P) is itself a pi-system.
A Dynkin system that is also a pi-system is a sigma-algebra: it is closed under arbitrary finite intersections, hence finite unions by complements, and any countable union can be disjointified before using closure under disjoint unions. Therefore λ(P)=σ(P), proving the lemma.

∇⋅(Bf)
(341)

The Poincaré-Bendixson theorem states that if a forward trajectory of a smooth planar system remains in a compact set and its nonempty omega-limit set contains no equilibrium point, then that omega-limit set is a periodic orbit.

At an equilibrium point of a dynamical system, the second equation gives
x(s−xy)=0.
(343)
The choice x=0 is impossible because then x˙=r>0. Hence y=s/x, and substitution into the first equation gives
0=r−(1+s)x+sx=r−x.
(344)
Thus the unique fixed point is
(x∗​,y∗​)=(r,rs​)​.
(345)
Choose
α=1+sr​​,
(346)
which satisfies 0<α<r. Let
R={(x,y):x≥α,0≤y≤αs​,x+y≤r+αs​}.
(347)
We check the direction of the vector field on its four edges.
On x=α,
x˙=r−(1+s)α+α2y=α2y≥0.
(348)
On y=0,
y˙​=sx>0.
(349)
On y=s/α, where x≥α,
y˙​=sx(1−αx​)≤0.
(350)
Finally, throughout the system,
x˙+y˙​=r−x.
(351)
On the sloping edge x+y=r+s/α, the bound y≤s/α implies x≥r, and hence x˙+y˙​≤0. Every boundary edge therefore points inward. Violations of the corresponding four inequalities are driven toward the boundary in the same order, so positive trajectories enter this compact trapping region and then remain there. This is the Brusselator trapping region.
The Jacobian matrix at the unique fixed point is
J∗​=(−(1+s)+2x∗​y∗​s−2x∗​y∗​​x∗2​−x∗2​​)=(s−1−s​r2−r2​).
(352)
Its determinant and trace are
detJ∗​=r2>0,trJ∗​=s−1−r2.
(353)
When s−1>r2, the trace is positive, so linear stability of a planar equilibrium shows that the fixed point is a repeller. It lies in the interior of R.
Choose a trajectory in R other than the equilibrium. Compactness of R gives a nonempty compact omega-limit set, and the repelling equilibrium cannot belong to that set. Since there are no other equilibria, the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem gives a periodic orbit. Hence
s−1>r2⟹the system has a periodic orbit.​
(354)
This is the Brusselator periodic-orbit criterion.

The microcanonical ensemble describes an isolated system at fixed energy E, volume V, and particle number N, assigning equal weight to accessible states in a narrow energy shell.
The canonical ensemble describes a system that can exchange energy with a heat reservoir at fixed temperature T, while V and N remain fixed. A microstate s has probability
ps​=Ze−βEs​​,Z=∑s​e−βEs​,β=kB​T1​.
(412)
The grand canonical ensemble allows exchange of both energy and particles at fixed T, V, and chemical potential μ. Its state weights are
ps​=Ξe−β(Es​−μNs​)​.
(413)
The choice is irrelevant for bulk thermodynamic observables in the thermodynamic limit when the system is additive, has sufficiently short-range interactions, and lies away from singular phase-coexistence regimes. Then relative energy and particle-number fluctuations vanish as the system size grows. These are the standard conditions for equivalence of statistical ensembles.

−∇p+μ∇2u=0,∇⋅u=0.
(457)
Taking the curl eliminates the pressure gradient and commutes with the Laplacian, so for the vorticity ω=∇×u,
∇2ω=0​.
(458)
This is the vorticity part of Harmonic pressure and vorticity in Stokes flow.
For a two-dimensional incompressible flow, choose the stream function convention
ux​=ψy​,uy​=−ψx​.

ωz​=∂x​uy​−∂y​ux​=−∇2ψ.
(460)
Applying the harmonic-vorticity equation gives
∇4ψ=0​,
(461)
the Biharmonic stream function for planar Stokes flow equation.

In the exterior domain r>a, the streamfunction obeys
∇4ψ=0​.
(462)
Using the Streamfunction in polar coordinates convention
ur​=r1​ψθ​,uθ​=−ψr​,
(463)
the no-slip condition on the stationary disk is
ur​(a,θ)=uθ​(a,θ)=0.
(464)
Thus ψ is constant on the disk and ψr​=0 there. Choose the arbitrary constant to be zero:
ψ(a,θ)=0,ψr​(a,θ)=0​.
(465)
The imposed shear u∞​=γyex​ has streamfunction
ψ∞​=2γ​y2=4γr2​(1−cos2θ).
(466)
The far-field condition is therefore
∇ψ−∇ψ∞​⟶0(r→∞)​.

Only the axisymmetric and cos2θ modes are needed. The exterior biharmonic forms compatible with the far-field velocity are
ψ0​(r)=4γ​r2+C0​logr+D0​,
(468)
ψ2​(r,θ)=(−4γ​r2+C2​+D2​r−2)cos2θ.
(469)
Terms r2logr and r4cos2θ are excluded because they would dominate the imposed shear.
The two conditions at r=a applied separately to each Fourier mode give
C0​=−2γa2​,D0​=−4γa2​+2γa2​loga,
(470)
C2​=2γa2​,D2​=−4γa4​.
(471)
Hence
ψ(r,θ)=4γ​[r2−a2−2a2logar​−(r2−2a2+r2a4​)cos2θ]​.
(472)
Direct differentiation gives ψ=ψr​=0 at r=a. At infinity the remaining disturbance velocity is O(r−1), so the imposed shear is recovered. This is the Biharmonic stream function for a fixed disk in planar shear.

The polar shear stress in a Newtonian fluid is
σrθ​=μ[r∂r∂​(ruθ​​)+r1​∂θ∂ur​​].
(473)
On r=a, no slip holds for every θ, so uθ​=0 and ∂θ​ur​=0. Therefore
σrθ​(a,θ)=μ∂r​uθ​(a,θ)=−μψrr​(a,θ).
(474)
Differentiating the solution from part (ii) gives
ψrr​(a,θ)=γ−2γcos2θ,
(475)
and hence
σrθ​(a,θ)=−μγ+2μγcos2θ​.
(476)
The moment arm and line element are both a, so the torque exerted by the fluid on the disk per unit axial length is
Tz​​=a2∫02π​σrθ​(a,θ)dθ=−2πμγa2​.​
(477)
For γ>0 the negative sign denotes the clockwise sense of the ambient shear rotation. This agrees with the hydrodynamic torque on a fixed disk in planar shear.

Let ρ′ and p′ be the density and pressure perturbations and let u be the velocity perturbation. The linear acoustics equations about a uniform quiescent state are
ρt′​+ρ0​∇⋅u=0,ρ0​ut​=−∇p′,p′=c02​ρ′.
(478)
The last relation is the homentropic pressure perturbation law.
Taking the scalar product of the momentum equation with u gives
∂t∂​(21​ρ0​∣u∣2)=−u⋅∇p′=−∇⋅(p′u)+p′∇⋅u.
(479)
The continuity and pressure relations imply
p′∇⋅u=−ρ0​c02​p′pt′​​=−∂t∂​(2ρ0​c02​p′2​).
(480)
Therefore the acoustic energy conservation law is
∂t∂​(K+W)+∇⋅I=0​,
(481)
with
K=21​ρ0​∣u∣2,W=2ρ0​c02​p′2​,I=p′u​.
(482)

If c0​≪ωa, then x≫1. The sphere is acoustically large, and
⟨K⟩∼⟨W⟩,∣⟨Ir​⟩∣∼c0​⟨K+W⟩.
(498)
Pressure and velocity are nearly in phase, so the near-surface field behaves locally like a progressive radiating wave. The power approaches
2πa2ρ0​ω2ϵ2c0​.
(499)
If c0​≫ωa, then x≪1. The sphere is acoustically compact, and
⟨K⟩⟨W⟩​∼x2≪1,∣⟨Ir​⟩∣c0​⟨K+W⟩​∼2x21​≫1.
(500)
The surface field is mainly reactive kinetic energy: pressure and velocity are nearly in quadrature, energy is stored and returned during each cycle, and only a small mean acoustic energy flux is radiated. The mean power scales as
⟨P⟩∼c0​2πρ0​ω4ϵ2a4​.​
(501)

At an interior grid point, the five-point finite difference method gives
∇2u(ih,jh,t)≈h21​(ui+1,j​+ui−1,j​+ui,j+1​+ui,j−1​−4uij​).
(502)
Let
T=​−21​1−2⋱​⋱⋱1​1−2​​∈Rm×m,
(503)
where the zero Dirichlet boundary values are already incorporated. Stack the unknowns with the y index varying fastest. Using the Kronecker product, define
Ax​=T⊗Im​,Ay​=Im​⊗T​.
(504)
Then the semidiscrete equation is
dtdu​=h21​(Ax​+Ay​)u,u(t)∈Rm2​.
(505)
Moreover,
Ax​Ay​=(T⊗I)(I⊗T)=T⊗T=(I⊗T)(T⊗I)=Ay​Ax​.
(506)
Thus the directional matrices commute, as in the five-point Dirichlet Laplacian as a Kronecker sum.

Because Ay​=I⊗T, this consists of m independent tridiagonal systems of dimension m. The Thomas algorithm solves each in O(m) operations, for a total of O(m2).
The second stage,
un+1=(I+μAx​)un+1/2,
(508)

ii OurBigBook.com
Eliminating the intermediate vector gives the amplification matrix
un+1=Cun,C=(I+μAx​)(I−μAy​)−1​.
(510)
The commuting real symmetric matrices admit simultaneous diagonalization in the orthonormal basis v(p,q) from the question. On this vector,
cpq​=1−μλq​1+μλp​​​,λj​=−4sin2(2jπh​).
(511)
Since the basis is orthonormal, stability in the discrete Euclidean norm is equivalent to ∣cpq​∣≤1 for every p,q.
Put
α=4sin22πh​,β=4cos22πh​.
(512)
Then −β≤λj​≤−α. The smallest denominator is 1+μα, while the largest numerator modulus occurs at an endpoint of this interval. The condition involving 1−μα is automatic, and the other is
∣1−μβ∣≤1+μα.
(513)
For m>1, this is equivalent to
μ(β−α)≤2.
(514)
Since β−α=4cos(πh), the exact finite-grid stability condition is
0<μ≤2cos(πh)1​​.
(515)
For m=1 there is only one mode and the method is stable for every μ>0. A simple grid-independent condition, and the limiting condition as h→0, is
0<μ≤21​​.
(516)
This is the stability limit of one-implicit-direction diffusion splitting.

(517)
The correction stage is
(I−μAx​)un+1=un+1−μAx​un.
(518)
Using Ax​Ay​=Ay​Ax​,
un+1−μAx​un​=[(I+μAx​)(I−μAy​)−1−μAx​]un=(I+μ2Ax​Ay​)(I−μAy​)−1un.​
(519)
Therefore
un+1=Dun,D=(I−μAx​)−1(I+μ2Ax​Ay​)(I−μAy​)−1​.
(520)
On the common eigenvector v(p,q), the eigenvalue of D is
dpq​=(1−μλp​)(1−μλq​)1+μ2λp​λq​​​.
(521)
Set a=−μλp​>0 and b=−μλq​>0. Then
dpq​=(1+a)(1+b)1+ab​.
(522)
Both numerator and denominator are positive, and
(1+a)(1+b)−(1+ab)=a+b>0.
(523)
Hence
0<dpq​<1
(524)
for every mode and every μ>0. Orthogonal diagonalization now gives ∥D∥2​<1, so the method is stable without a time-step restriction. This is the unconditionally stable corrected directional diffusion splitting.
